description:
Hi! I'm Diar (15 yo), leading team SpaceScout. I do backend (C++/Python), electronics, and management. Our goal is finding Earth analogs for Moon/Mars missions by systematically analyzing geology, mineralogy, and atmospheric processes to see where analogies work or break down.

Looking for team members:

Python Developers

GIS Analysts  

Designers 

Join SpaceScout to accelerate space exploration
summary:
We developed a comparative framework identifying terrestrial analogs for Columbus Crater, a Martian paleolake basin that held a ~900 m deep lake during the Late Noachian before drying into evaporite salts, sulfates (including gypsum), and clays. Our team, SpaceScout, compared two Earth sites — the Aralkum (the desiccated bed of the Aral Sea) and the adjacent Ustyurt Plateau — against Columbus Crater across eight parameters: terrain, temperature, pressure/atmosphere, geology and minerals, dust and wind, water and ice, gravity, and radiation, using real climate, geochemical, and radiation data (including our own measurements).

Rather than claiming a perfect match, we rate each parameter’s similarity (strong/partial/weak) and explicitly flag where the analogy breaks down — gravity, atmospheric density, and radiation differ sharply from Mars.

This matters because active, ongoing analogs like Aralkum let researchers study lake-desiccation and salt-crust formation processes in real time, test rover navigation, drilling, and sampling methods on flat salt plains and escarpments, and validate mineral-detection techniques — directly supporting Mars (and future Moon base) mission preparation with low-cost, accessible field sites.
details:
Based on the project document, here's a detailed response to these questions:

What does it do / how does it work?

The project builds a comparative framework that benchmarks two terrestrial sites — the Aralkum (the dried bed of the Aral Sea) and the adjacent Ustyurt Plateau — against Columbus Crater on Mars, a paleolake basin that held a ~900 m deep lake in the Late Noachian before desiccating into evaporite salts, sulfates (gypsum), and clays. The team gathered quantitative data across eight comparison categories — terrain/slope, temperature, pressure/atmosphere, geology/minerals, dust/wind, water/ice, gravity, and radiation — pulling from published planetary science papers (e.g., Wray et al. 2011 on Columbus Crater), Kazhydromet meteorological datasets, and the team's own field radiation measurements (gamma data collected at Beyneu and the Aral Sea). Each parameter is then rated qualitatively — strong / partial / weak / no data — against Columbus Crater, producing a transparent similarity assessment rather than a single composite "match score."

What benefits does it have?

  • Identifies accessible, low-cost analog sites close to the team's home region (Kazakhstan/Uzbekistan) instead of relying only on remote/expensive analog sites elsewhere in the world.
  • Gives mission planners a parameter-by-parameter breakdown, so they know exactly which tests each site is good for (e.g., Aralkum/Ustyurt for dust, salt-crust, and drilling studies) and which it is not suited for (gravity, radiation, atmospheric density tests).
  • Combines real, current environmental monitoring data (not just historical literature), making the comparison empirically grounded.

Intended impact

To support Mars (and future lunar base) mission preparation by providing validated terrestrial test sites for rover navigation, drilling, sampling, and mineral-detection instrument calibration — and to advance scientific understanding of how saline lake systems desiccate, which is directly relevant to interpreting Mars' paleolake history.

Tools, languages, hardware/software used

  • Data sources/software: Kazhydromet climate database (ecodata.kz), satellite imagery tools (NASA Worldview, NASA Trek) for site identification and visualization, spreadsheet tools (.xlsx) for processing meteorological and radiation datasets.
  • Hardware: field radiation measurement equipment (gamma dosimeters) used to collect original data at Beyneu and Aral Sea sites.
  • Documentation: structured written report (Word/.docx) consolidating literature review, data tables, and source citations.

How is the project creative?

  • Instead of using a single generic analog site, it performs a rigorous, multi-parameter side-by-side comparison of two distinct Earth environments against one specific Mars feature, explicitly scoring agreement and disagreement per parameter.
  • It actively collects new field data (radiation measurements) rather than relying solely on secondary literature, strengthening the analog case with fresh evidence.
  • It is transparent about limitations (missing lunar data, approximate values, geographic mismatch between Ustyurt data and Mangystau station data) — a deliberately honest, scientifically rigorous framing rather than an overstated claim.

Factors the team considered

  • Geological plausibility (comparable deposits: evaporite salts, gypsum, clays).
  • Data availability and reliability, clearly flagging where proxy data (e.g., Mangystau station standing in for Ustyurt) had to be used.
  • Scale differences (Aral Sea's 1083 km³ volume vs. Columbus's estimated 6000 km³).
  • Environmental factors unsuitable for direct analogy (gravity, atmospheric pressure/composition, radiation levels), which they did not try to force into the analogy.
  • Practical mission-relevance, prioritizing parameters useful for rover testing, instrument calibration, and sampling procedure development.
projectRefs: Mars’ Surface Radiation Environment Measured with the Mars Science Laboratory’s Curiosity Rover
